---
title: "2. Rare and emerging markers: k13 R561H in East Africa"
description: >
  Mapping a marker that most surveys never find: the artemisinin
  partial-resistance mutation k13 R561H, from Rwanda into north-western
  Tanzania and south-western Uganda.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
# site builds: GADM files downloaded earlier, if STAREAL_GADM_CACHE names a folder of them
local({
  cache <- Sys.getenv("STAREAL_GADM_CACHE")
  if (nzchar(cache)) {
    dir.create(file.path(tempdir(), "gadm"), showWarnings = FALSE)
    file.copy(list.files(cache, pattern = "^gadm41_", full.names = TRUE), file.path(tempdir(), "gadm"))
  }
})
```

The kelch13 R561H mutation confers artemisinin partial resistance. In the
data used here it appears first in Rwanda, and later in north-western
Tanzania and south-western Uganda. A marker like this differs from crt K76T
in [tutorial 1](crt76t.html) in three ways:

- **most surveys find nothing**, so the data are mostly zeros;
- **the signal is local and recent**: a few areas, in the last decade;
- **the questions are about thresholds**: where is prevalence probably
  above a level that matters for policy?

This tutorial maps R561H across five countries around Lake Victoria:
Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya. It moves quickly through the
steps of tutorial 1 and dwells on what changes.

```{r packages}
library(stareal)
```

## 1. The data

The same STAVE object as in tutorial 1, and the prevalence of R561H:

```{r stave}
url <- paste0("https://github.com/IDEELResearch/scrub/raw/2d85d021efe1c93dc55300610d944c9fbaf4af1a/",
              "analysis/data-out/stave_data_2026.03.17.rds")
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
download.file(url, tmp, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
stave <- suppressWarnings(readRDS(tmp))
p <- stave$get_prevalence("k13:561:H")
p <- p[p$denominator > 0, ]
```

Most surveys find no R561H. Those zeros are what tell the model where the
mutation is absent, so they must be kept. `get_prevalence()` keeps them: it
counts every survey that genotyped codon 561.

The frame is the first-level units of the five countries, from GADM, with
the large lakes cut out as in tutorial 1, here in an equal-area projection
centred on Lake Victoria. The surveys are selected by location, as in
tutorial 1:

```{r frame, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
adm1 <- sf::st_as_sf(geodata::gadm(c("RWA", "BDI", "TZA", "UGA", "KEN"), level = 1, path = tempdir(),
                                   version = "4.1", resolution = 2))
lakes <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(scale = 10, type = "lakes", category = "physical",
                                    returnclass = "sf", destdir = tempdir())
crs <- "+proj=laea +lat_0=-3 +lon_0=34 +units=m"
adm1 <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_transform(adm1, crs))
lakes <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_transform(lakes, crs))
lakes <- lakes[as.numeric(sf::st_area(lakes)) > 1e9, ]
water <- sf::st_intersection(sf::st_union(lakes), sf::st_union(adm1))
adm1 <- sf::st_difference(adm1, water)
adm1 <- adm1[adm1$ENGTYPE_1 != "Water body", ]           # what is left of Uganda's lake units
fr <- areal_frame(adm1, id = "GID_1", groups = c(country = "COUNTRY"), link_within = "country",
                  verbose = FALSE)
pts <- sf::st_transform(sf::st_as_sf(p, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326), fr$crs_planar)
surveys <- p[lengths(sf::st_is_within_distance(pts, adm1, dist = 10000)) > 0, ]
```

Yearly steps from 2010. A rare marker has few positive surveys, and a year
pools them into better-informed cells; the emergence unfolds over years,
not months.

```{r data}
tf <- time_frame(2010, 2024, "year")
d <- areal_data(surveys, fr, tf, y = "numerator", k = "denominator",
                coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), date = "collection_day")
d
```

By country, from the units the surveys fall in:

```{r by-country}
used <- d$surveys[is.na(d$surveys$.excluded), ]
country <- fr$groups$country[match(used$.id, fr$ids)]
tab <- data.frame(surveys = c(table(country)),
                  with_R561H = c(tapply(used$numerator > 0, country, sum)),
                  positive = c(tapply(used$numerator, country, sum)),
                  tested = c(tapply(used$denominator, country, sum)))
tab
```

```{r data-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(d)
```

Rwanda has few of the surveys but most of the R561H: it was found in
`r tab["Rwanda", "with_R561H"]` of Rwanda's `r tab["Rwanda", "surveys"]`
surveys. Tanzania has by far the most surveys, and finds R561H in
`r tab["Tanzania", "with_R561H"]`. Uganda finds it in
`r tab["Uganda", "with_R561H"]` and Kenya in none. Burundi has only
`r tab["Burundi", "tested"]` people tested, all in 2013.

## 2. Fitting

A first fit with the defaults:

```{r pilot, message = FALSE}
pilot <- fit_areal(d)
diagnose(pilot)$checks
```

It fails: the hyperparameters' effective sample size is well below 400.
Mostly-zero data say little about each cell, and the hyperparameters mix
slowly. The remedy is a longer run, here more than three times the default
length:

```{r fit, message = FALSE}
fit <- fit_areal(d, control = list(n_iter = 10000, n_burn = 2000))
diagnose(fit)$checks
summary(fit)
```

```{r traces, fig.height = 6}
plot(fit)
```

```{r fixed-effects, include = FALSE}
fe <- setNames(summary(fit)$table$mean, summary(fit)$table$variable)
```

```{r fit-numbers, include = FALSE}
tr <- summary(fit)$table[summary(fit)$table$variable == "trend", ]
```

The longer run passes every check. Compared with crt K76T:

- The `intercept` is the logit prevalence in the middle of the window
  (2017), before the field: about `r round(fe[["intercept"]], 1)`, or
  `r signif(100 * plogis(fe[["intercept"]]), 1)`%. That is the regional
  baseline: the mutation is absent from most of the region.
- The `trend` is positive but uncertain: its interval runs from
  `r round(tr$q2.5, 1)` to `r round(tr$q97.5, 1)`. The rise is local, in and
  around Rwanda, so the field carries it rather than a trend for the whole
  region.
- `sigma` is large. The field has to carry a local emergence: tens of
  percent in a few units, against near zero in most.
- `sigma_n` is large too. Unit-years depart from the smooth field by more
  than it can explain: neighbouring units, or one unit in consecutive
  years, can differ sharply.

## 3. Where has R561H spread?

The probability that prevalence exceeds 5% is asked for with `exceedance`:

```{r predict}
pr <- predict(fit, groups = "country", exceedance = 0.05, verbose = FALSE)
```

Country trends, with the surveys and their exact binomial intervals:

```{r countries, fig.height = 5}
plot(pr, group = "country", ids = c("Rwanda", "Tanzania", "Uganda", "Burundi", "Kenya"))
```

```{r country-table}
subset(pr$groups$country, time %in% c("2016", "2020", "2024"),
       select = c(id, time, mean, q50, q2.5, q97.5, p_gt_0.05))
```

Maps of the posterior mean, and of the probability that prevalence exceeds
5%, with the lakes drawn as water:

```{r maps, fig.height = 6.5}
m <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("2016", "2020", "2024"), function(y) sf::st_as_sf(pr, time = y)))
lake <- geom_sf(data = sf::st_sf(water), fill = "#bcd6ea", colour = NA)
g1 <- ggplot(m) + geom_sf(aes(fill = mean), colour = NA) + lake + facet_wrap(~time) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("R561H\nprevalence", option = "magma") + theme_void()
g2 <- ggplot(m) + geom_sf(aes(fill = p_gt_0.05), colour = NA) + lake + facet_wrap(~time) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("P(prevalence\n> 5%)", limits = c(0, 1), option = "magma") + theme_void()
patchwork::wrap_plots(g1, g2, ncol = 1)
```

In 2016 the probability of exceeding 5% is moderate at most, in Rwanda.
By 2020 it is high across much of Rwanda. By 2024 it reaches across the
borders, into north-western Tanzania, south-western Uganda and northern
Burundi.

Which units are more likely than not above 5% in 2024, and what data stand
behind each?

```{r hotspots}
hot <- subset(pr$area, time == "2024" & p_gt_0.05 > 0.5)
hot$name <- adm1$NAME_1[match(hot$id, adm1$GID_1)]
hot$tested <- tapply(pr$area$k, pr$area$id, sum)[hot$id]     # over all years
hot$positive <- tapply(pr$area$y, pr$area$id, sum)[hot$id]
hot <- hot[order(-hot$p_gt_0.05), ]
hot[, c("name", "country", "mean", "q2.5", "q97.5", "p_gt_0.05", "tested", "positive")]
```

```{r hot-groups, include = FALSE}
with_data <- hot$name[hot$tested >= 100]
no_data <- hot$name[hot$tested == 0]
```

The table says two different things:

- **Some rest on data**, with a hundred or more tested:
  `r paste(with_data, collapse = ", ")`. These are Rwanda's provinces, and
  the units across its borders where R561H has been found.
- **Some have no surveys at all**: `r paste(no_data, collapse = ", ")`.
  Their probabilities come from their neighbours.

With a rare marker, a map of the mean or of an exceedance probability shows
where the model cannot rule the marker out as much as where it is. Read it
with the map of the data and the intervals.

## 4. What the model assumes, and when to doubt the map

```{r burundi, include = FALSE}
bdi_24 <- subset(pr$groups$country, id == "Burundi" & time == "2024")
```

- **Neighbours fill the gaps.** The field is smooth in space, so a unit with
  no surveys borrows from those around it. Burundi lies between Rwanda and
  Kagera, and has `r tab["Burundi", "tested"]` people tested, all in 2013.
  Its mean reaches `r round(100 * bdi_24$mean)`% by 2024, with an interval
  from `r round(100 * bdi_24$q2.5, 1)`% to `r round(100 * bdi_24$q97.5)`%.
  That is not a finding about Burundi. It says that its neighbours' data
  cannot rule R561H out there.
- **One variance for the whole region.** The field is stationary: the same
  `sigma`, `rho_s` and `rho_t` in every area and year. An emergence is a
  local, growing departure, and the model accommodates it with a large
  `sigma`. That variance then applies everywhere, which is why unsurveyed
  units have such wide intervals.
- **After the last survey.** Rwanda's surveys stop in 2023 in these data, so
  2024 there is extrapolated, and its interval widens.
- **Where the surveys were made.** Studies of an emerging marker are often
  sited where resistance is suspected, for example after treatment
  failures. The model assumes that survey locations tell it nothing about
  prevalence. If studies chase the mutation, the surveyed units overstate
  their neighbours.
- **A zero is worth its sample size.** 0 of 50 is not unusual when
  prevalence is 5%: it happens `r round(100 * dbinom(0, 50, 0.05))`% of
  the time. The long grey bars in the country plot are surveys of one or a
  few infections: they say almost nothing. The binomial likelihood weighs
  each zero by its denominator, but many small zeros do not prove absence.
